title: The Teacher Wishlist That Can't Be Fulfilled Through Amazon 2026
author: Beth Geoghegan
source: Freedom In Education, republished on Substack (bgeoghegan4.substack.com), September 2,
summary: Beth Geoghegan reframes the familiar teacher Amazon wishlist by arguing the items that actually optimize student learning most cannot be purchased online at all: daily parent-child reading time, limited screen time, enforced screen-free bedtimes, and reliable daily attendance. Her central evidentiary anchor is the finding that children read five books a day from birth enter kindergarten having heard roughly 1.4 million more words than children never read to, which she connects to cognitive science's background-knowledge research via Natalie Wexler's argument that knowledge "sticks best to other related knowledge" and Blake Harvard's spiderweb metaphor, more connected knowledge networks catch and hold more new information, while sparser ones let it slip through. Geoghegan is explicit that these home practices don't just build vocabulary but also shape a child's emotional relationship to reading, easing the teacher's separate task of persuading reluctant readers that reading matters, and she extends the same logic to screen time and sleep, both of which the research she cites ties directly to attention and academic performance in the classroom. The piece closes by naming attendance as a non-negotiable precondition beneath all of it: no instructional strategy can work for a child who is not physically present.
points: The 1.4-million-word gap between children read to five times daily from birth and children never read to functions as the piece's load-bearing statistic, translating an abstract 'reading matters' claim into a concrete, cited disparity in word exposure before kindergarten even begins.

Blake Harvard's spiderweb metaphor for background knowledge, a web with more connections catches more, one with fewer breaks more easily, gives parents (and teachers reading this) a vivid mental model for why reading aloud builds compounding rather than merely additive advantage.

Geoghegan explicitly separates the cognitive effect of home reading (vocabulary and background knowledge) from its emotional effect (positive association with reading), arguing the second effect does real classroom work for teachers by 'alleviating the need to convince reluctant children why reading is important.'

Naming daily attendance as the final, unglamorous item on the list functions as the piece's structural keystone: it makes explicit that every other item, reading time, screen limits, sleep, is moot if a child is not physically present for the instruction those practices are meant to prepare them for.
quotes: Research shows that young children whose parents read them five books a day enter kindergarten having heard about 1.4 million more words than kids who were never read to. Those words equate to knowledge, and, thanks to cognitive science, we know that background knowledge is key to learning and connecting new knowledge.

The more knowledge a child starts with, the more likely she is to acquire yet more knowledge. She'll read more and understand and retain information better. Because knowledge, like Velcro, sticks best to other related knowledge.

An actual web that has more connections and links will be much stronger than a web with fewer and will do a better job at catching bugs. The web that has very few attachments is more likely to break and simply doesn't have the same ability to trap any bugs that may fly into it.

Additionally, children who are read to regularly at home tend to develop positive attitudes toward reading and learning, and tend to associate reading with happy, pleasant experiences. This practice helps classroom teachers by alleviating the need to convince reluctant children why reading is important.
Research has shown that excessive screen time can impair attention spans in school-aged children, potentially impacting their academic performance.
When students aren't in school, teachers can't teach them. Enrolling your children in school is futile if you don't actually ensure they attend.
